The evening before
Tuesday, 31 March 2037, evening. Tomorrow, at seven in the morning, Leo drives on his own for the first time, without an instructor. He's sitting with Ludwig in the kitchen.
Grandad, were you nervous before your first solo run?
Nineteen sixty-nine. I didn't sleep all night. I imagined I'd forgotten everything. Every stop, every signal.
And? Had you forgotten?
No. As soon as I sat down in the cab, it all came back. You don't forget what you've practised every day. You only forget that you know it.
That sounds like something Elif would have said to Elena.
Elif has it from Grete. And Grete from Mr Wendland. And I have it from all three. That's how it is with good sentences. They're passed on, like a cup.
Tomorrow I'll pass Kastanienallee. At twelve minutes past seven. Will you be at the window?
I'm eighty-eight. I wake up at five anyway. Of course I'll be at the window.
And how many times should I ring the bell?
That's for you to decide. You're a tram driver now. But if you ask me: once is for joy. Twice is for those who can't stand at the window any more.

Sieben Uhr zwölf

On Wednesday, the first of April two thousand and thirty-seven, at five forty-three, Leo Brandt stood in the Lichtenberg depot in front of an M1 tram, car number nine-zero-two-four, and breathed. Like his grandfather sixty-eight years before, he hadn't slept all night. He had imagined he'd forgotten everything. Every stop. Every signal. Every set of points between Hackescher Markt and Pankow. At three he had switched on the light and gone over the route in his head once more, stop by stop, and when he got to Rosenthaler Platz he was no longer sure whether Zionskirchstraße or Schwedter Straße came next. He had looked it up. It was Zionskirchstraße. Of course. He knew it. He had only forgotten that he knew it.

Mr Schäfer wasn't there. That was the strangest thing. For six months he had sat next to Leo in the cab every morning, silent, with his moustache and his clipboard, and Leo had got so used to him that the empty space next to the control lever now felt like a hole in the world. On Friday, their last day together, Mr Schäfer had said exactly three sentences in farewell, which for him was a long speech. “You're ready. I have nothing more to teach you. Give my regards to your grandfather.” Then he had shaken Leo's hand and left, and only later did Leo notice that Mr Schäfer had slipped something into his jacket pocket: a slip of paper on which was written, in very neat handwriting: “Like a cup of coffee.”

Leo climbed into the cab. He put the old white cup with the BVB logo on the shelf next to the screen, where it had stood since October, empty, as a witness. Next to it he stuck Mr Schäfer's slip of paper, under the cardboard with Elif's four points, which was still hanging there. He put his grandfather's small grey notebook, the 1966 service regulations with Ingrid's drawing on the last page, in the compartment under the control lever. Then he reported to control, in a calm voice, as he had practised. “Control, this is nine-zero-two-four, M1, driver Brandt, ready to depart.” And a voice he knew answered. Not the usual control voice, but an older one, deeper, with a slight laugh in it. “Nine-zero-two-four, this is Wolff. Safe journey, Mr Brandt. I'm listening in personally today.”

At six twenty-eight Leo set off from Hackescher Markt, with fourteen passengers who had no idea they were sitting in a historic tram. Not historic like the Tatra in the museum. Historic like a first day. He set off the way you carry a cup of coffee filled to the brim. Nobody noticed anything. A woman was reading the newspaper. A student was asleep with his head against the window. Two children with school bags were quietly arguing over a sandwich. At Rosenthaler Platz twelve people got on, and Leo waited until the last one was in, an old man with a walking stick, who sat down slowly and nodded through the glass towards the cab. Leo nodded back. Then Zionskirchstraße. Of course, Zionskirchstraße. Then Kastanienallee.

In the café «Bei Ingrid» on Ingrid-Brandt-Platz there were more people at seven in the morning than had ever been there on an ordinary Wednesday at that hour. Lena had opened at five, as usual, but this morning she hadn't baked rolls; she had made coffee, one big pot of tea after another, for everyone who came. And everyone came. Andrei, with binoculars borrowed from Michael Kühn. Mara and Jakob with Ingrid Hilde, two years old, in pyjamas under her coat, who didn't know why everyone was up so early but found it exciting. Elif, who had written her teacher a note excusing her absence, in bureaucratic German, beginning with the sentence: “As a result of a family event of historic importance …” Abena, who had the day off and had come wearing Grete's black hat, “because Grete has to be there”. And Dr Vogt, who had come straight from his night shift and said he was awake anyway.

Hotte came last, at five past seven, with his two walking sticks and his tram driver's cap, and with a piece of news he announced at once: he had bought, for the first time in his life, a mobile phone. Yesterday. So that he could “record the thing”. He held it up, a big, simple phone for older people, with huge buttons, and then admitted that he didn't yet know how to film with it. Elif showed him, in thirty seconds. Hotte was impressed. “This kid”, he said to Ludwig, “in one year she's taught a Romanian woman German, a boy the piano and a ninety-two-year-old the phone. What's she doing next year? Chancellor?” Elif blushed. Ludwig said nothing. He was sitting at the window, in his seat, with his cup of coffee in his hand, looking at the street. At the rails. As they had taught him in nineteen sixty-eight. Not at the people. At the rails.

At eleven minutes past seven Andrei saw the tram through the binoculars, down at the corner, at the Schwedter Straße stop. “It's coming”, he said, and the café went so quiet that you could hear the coffee machine. Everyone crowded to the big windows. Ingrid Hilde sat on Jakob's shoulders. Hotte held the phone up, the wrong way round, and Elif turned it round for him without a word. Lena stood behind Ludwig's chair and put her hands on his shoulders. And Ludwig stood up. Slowly, leaning on his stick, with Lena's hand on his arm. He went to the window, very close to the glass, the way he had stood sixty-nine years before at the window of another tram, on his first day, when a man called Wilke had told him not to look at the people.

The tram came up Kastanienallee, yellow, with the number nine-zero-two-four on its side and the display “M1 Pankow” above the windscreen, slowly, much more slowly than necessary, like someone passing a place they love and wanting to look at it one more time. At Ingrid-Brandt-Platz, in front of the café, in front of the windows behind which twenty-three people were standing, it slowed down, not to a stop, because there was no stop here, but almost. And in the cab sat Leo, in uniform, alone, looking towards the window. Not at the rails. For the first time in six months, not at the rails. He saw his grandfather. And his grandfather raised his hand, very slowly, and placed it on the glass.

Leo rang the bell. Once. Bright and clear, the sound of a modern tram, which rang out along Kastanienallee, along the houses, right up to the roofs, from which the first pigeons took off. In the café someone cheered, probably Hotte, and Ingrid Hilde clapped her hands on Jakob's shoulders. Once. For joy. For the first day. For everyone standing at the window. And then, after a moment, when the tram had almost passed the café, Leo rang once more. Softer. Longer. And Ludwig, at the window, knew who the second time was for. For Ingrid, who had taught him books and commas. For Grete, who lived under the chestnut tree in the courtyard and had said she wanted to hear when someone rang. For Friedrich, for Mr Wendland, for Mr Wilke, for Erna. For all those who could no longer stand at the window.

Nobody in the café said anything for a long time. The tram had already disappeared round the bend, towards Schönhauser Allee, towards Pankow, and the sound of the bell still hung in the air, like a note that doesn't want to stop after the key has been released. Then Elif said, quietly, to nobody: “Twice.” And Hotte, who was still holding the phone up although there was nothing more to film, lowered it and said, in a voice nobody in the café had ever heard from him, rough and very quiet: “Erna would've cried. Not me.” He wiped his eyes with his sleeve. “Just got something in my eye. A pigeon.” Nobody contradicted him. Lena took his hand. And Ingrid Hilde, on Jakob's shoulders, shouted a word she had only known for a week and that nobody had taught her, loud and clear, and everyone laughed, because it was exactly the right word: “Nochmal!” Once more!

Leo drove on. Up Schönhauser Allee, past Eberswalder Straße, where the traffic grew heavier, and then, at the Milastraße stop, he saw him. A nine-year-old boy, in a red jacket he had grown out of by now, with a school bag on his back, holding the hand of a woman Leo recognised at once. Jonas. He was standing at the edge of the platform, not too close, but exactly behind the white line, as he had been taught, and when the tram stopped, he looked towards the cab and recognised Leo. He didn't say anything. He just raised his hand, like a grown-up, and Leo lifted two fingers from the control lever, and then Jonas got on, with his mother, sat down in the seat just behind the cab and rode to school, three stops, without a word, and got off, and waved once more. That evening Leo didn't tell anyone about it except Ludwig. Some things, he thought, belong only in a cab.

In Sibiu, Elena saw the video an hour later, in the kitchen, with Dan. Hotte had sent it, with his new phone, to all the numbers Elif had saved for him, and it was, as Elena noted with a laugh, the worst video ever filmed on Kastanienallee: it shook, it was half upside down, you saw more of the ceiling than of the tram and you mostly heard Hotte breathing. But you could also hear the bell. Once. And then, after a pause, a second time. Dan watched it three times, without saying anything. Then he got up, went to the shelf, took his old German exercise book, opened it at page eight, the first blank page, and wrote, slowly, in his big, clumsy handwriting, in German: “Der Junge fährt. Zweimal klingeln.” Elena didn't correct anything. It was, she thought, the best sentence Dan had ever written.

In the evening, when Leo came into the café after eight hours on duty, tired, with the white cup in one hand and the grey notebook in the other, Ludwig was waiting for him, at the table by the window, alone, with two cups of coffee. Leo sat down. They drank in silence for a while. Then Ludwig asked him how it had been. And Leo told him. About the depot at five forty-three. About Kurt Wolff's voice from control. About the old man at Rosenthaler Platz who had nodded. About the children with the sandwich. About Kastanienallee, and the window, and the hand on the glass. “I rang twice”, he said. “I didn't think about it. I just did it.” Ludwig nodded. “That's how it is”, he said. “You think you have to remember everything. And then, when the moment comes, your hand knows by itself.”

Then Ludwig took something out of his jacket pocket and put it on the table. It was the small, rough wooden bird with only one wing that grandmother Viorica had given him in Sibiu, the first bird Andrei's grandfather had carved at fourteen, clumsily, without knowing that fifty-two more would follow. Ludwig pushed it across the table to Leo. “I got it from someone who knew that beginnings are more important than the end”, he said. “Put it in your cab. Next to the cup.” Leo took the bird and looked at it for a long time. “It's only got one wing”, he said. Ludwig smiled. “Yes”, he said. “You have to add the second one yourself. A little every day. That's how it is with birds, and with tram drivers, and with languages.” He finished his coffee and stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick. “It's not the end, Leo”, he said at the door. “It's just the next stop.” And then, on his way out, he rang the brass bell, as he did every evening. Once. For joy. And once for all those who are listening.
